No. Our pre-registered test refuted the idea that Qloo taste data reliably predicts where a Korean cafe should open.

For finding underserved blocks, Qloo’s raw taste score had an AUC of 0.653, compared with 0.742 for existing restaurant count. The taste signal also appears to reflect nearby Korean venues: Korean presence AUC fell from 0.893 to 0.693 when blocks within 500 m of Korean restaurants were excluded.

Use Qloo to describe the audience and shape positioning, menu, and branding—not to select the lease. For opening decisions, prioritize city-records lease scores and local supply/competition.

No. Our pre-registered test refuted that use.

Qloo taste was a weak predictor of unserved demand: raw taste had a median AUC of 0.653, versus 0.742 for existing restaurant count. Peer-lift taste reached 0.579 and beat the restaurant-count baseline in only 1 of 14 cuisines. For Korean specifically, the signal largely reflects proximity to existing Korean restaurants; its AUC fell from 0.893 to 0.693 after nearby blocks were removed.

Use Qloo to describe the audience and shape the cafe’s positioning—not to decide where to open. Lease quality and existing supply should drive the location choice.

No. In our pre-registered test, Qloo taste did not reliably predict where a Korean cafe should open.

For blocks without existing Korean restaurants, raw taste reached AUC 0.653, while restaurant count reached 0.742. Peer-lift taste reached only 0.579 and outperformed restaurant count for 1 of 14 cuisines. The Korean signal also weakened from AUC 0.893 to 0.693 when blocks within 500 m of Korean restaurants were excluded, suggesting Qloo reflects nearby existing venues more than unmet demand.

Use Qloo to shape the audience, menu, and positioning—not to choose the lease. Lease selection should rely on city-records scores and competition data.
